title: Calcium tunes snail mucus-based materials to multiple functions.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Found the only deposit (PRIDE PXD065814, a public proteomics archive) and downloaded all three processed files: 4896_proteinGroups.txt (519 KB, 689 rows x 126 columns), Orbi4896_grouped_AggregatedBySnailIDs...txt (729 KB, 757 rows x 128 columns) and mqpar.xml. Counted samples (10 label-free runs, columns named only '01'-'10'), non-zero LFQ (label-free quantification) values per run (185-669 proteins), 79 contaminant and 11 reverse-database flags, and confirmed MaxQuant's experiment names are bare numbers with no mucus-type annotation. Also confirmed the paper is not in PubMed Central, has no supplementary files retrievable via Europe PMC, and that Zenodo and Edmond (the Max Planck data repository) hold no matching dataset.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That five distinct mucus types were studied, that collagen VI is the main structural protein, and that amorphous calcium carbonate granules are added during secretion - all from the abstract and the PRIDE project description. No rheology, X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy or calcium-content measurements are deposited anywhere I could find, so every physical property in the paper is text-only.

a1_downloadable.note: PRIDE PXD065814 is fully public, no login. I downloaded the two processed tables and the MaxQuant parameter file over plain HTTPS.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL, verified in the files. There is no label column of any kind. The 10 mass-spec runs are named only '01'-'10'; which run came from which of the five mucus types is in no deposited file (the submission is PRIDE type 'PARTIAL', so there is no sample-to-run mapping), and no measured property (adhesion strength, stiffness, calcium content) appears as a column. The target would have to be reconstructed by reading figures in a paywalled paper.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAIL, verified. Protein identity is given as Cepaea nemoralis gene-model IDs (e.g. Cnem011193-RA_True_44) from a six-frame translation of an unannotated whole-genome shotgun assembly. No amino-acid sequences are in the deposit, and those IDs resolve to no public FASTA, so sequence features cannot be obtained.

a4_units_stated.note: MaxQuant column names carry units where applicable ('Mol. weight [kDa]', 'Sequence coverage [%]'); LFQ intensity is the standard unitless normalized abundance. Units are not the problem here.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL, verified. The unit of observation is the mass-spec run and there are exactly 10, covering five mucus types (so roughly two replicates each). The 689 protein groups are features, not independent labelled examples. Far below the ~400 minimum even for classification.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Processed tables total 1.3 MB. The 10 raw mass-spec files are ~2 GB each (~20 GB total) but are raw data we would never download.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Nothing to contradict: the abstract gives no protein count. PRIDE's file listing matched the files I downloaded byte for byte; 689 protein groups in proteinGroups.txt and 757 rows in the aggregated table are internally consistent.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAIL by absence rather than circularity. There is no label to trace. The one thing resembling an annotation, the 'GeneName' column, is itself a computational transfer of names from the ten best BLAST-style hits in other species (e.g. 'Col6a5:Col6a6:Col6a4:COL14A1:...'), so using it as a target would mean learning a homology search's output, not biology.

honest_claim_h3: No honest claim is possible: with 10 unlabelled mass-spectrometry runs and no measured material property in any deposited file, any model would be describing two replicates per group rather than learning a relationship.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the protein make-up of snail slime to predict which job that slime does.
plain_idea.train_on: What a model would see: the abundance of each of 689 protein groups in a slime sample, measured by mass spectrometry. There are only 10 such samples in total, which is the fatal problem.
plain_idea.predict: Which of five mucus types the sample is (lubricating trail slime, adhesive, defensive, protective, or the dried winter seal), or ideally a physical property such as stiffness or calcium content. Neither the type nor any physical property is recorded in the deposited data.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Biomaterials groups designing stimuli-responsive adhesives would like to know which protein-plus-mineral recipes give which mechanical behaviour. This dataset is far too small to tell them, but a larger version across many mollusc species and mucus types would be genuinely new.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: classify snail mucus type, or regress a mechanical property, from mass-spectrometry protein abundances. Dies on sample size (10 runs) and on the complete absence of both a sample-type annotation and any measured material property in the deposit.

effort.compute_note: Measured, not estimated: the two processed tables are 1.3 MB combined and load into pandas in under a second. Embedding and cross-validation times are null because no modellable table can be built - there is no label and no protein sequence.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the quantification columns in the PRIDE table. Ten 'LFQ intensity' columns named '01'-'10' kills the project in one minute, before reading a word of the paper.

verdict_reason: Ten mass-spec runs, no label column anywhere, and no protein sequences - fails A2, A3, A5 and A8. The deposit (PRIDE PXD065814) contains only a MaxQuant protein-abundance table for 689 protein groups across 10 label-free runs covering five mucus types; the run-to-mucus-type mapping is absent from every deposited file, and the paper's actual findings (calcium carbonate content, mechanical behaviour, X-ray diffraction) are not deposited at all, on Zenodo or Edmond either. Scientifically appealing, structurally unmodellable. Parts B-J were not scored because a Part A killer failed.
